prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

No classes here! Why, that is idle talk. The village beau sneers at the country boor; The importuning mendicants who walk Our cites’ streets despise the parish poor. The daily toiler at some noisy loom Holds back her garments from the kitchen aid. Meanwhile the latter leans upon her broom, Unconscious of the bow the laundress made. The grocer’s daughter eyes the farmer’s lass With haughty glances; and the lawyer’s wife Would pay no visits to the trading class, If policy were not her creed in life. The merchant’s son nods coldly at the clerk; The proud possessor of a pedigree Ignores the youth whose father rose by work; The title-seeking maiden scorns all three. The aristocracy of blood looks down Upon the “nouveau riche”; and in disdain, The lovers of the intellectual frown On both, and worship at the shrine of brain. “No classes here,” the clergyman has said; “We are one family.” Yet see his rage And horror when his favorite son would wed Some pure and pretty player on the stage. It is the vain but natural way Of vaunting our weak selves, our pride, our worth! Not till the long delayed millennial day Shall we behold “no classes” on God’s earth.

outputs.L1:
“No classes here!” Why, that is idle talk.  
The village beau sneers at the country boor;  
The importuning mendicants who walk  
Our cities’ streets despise the parish poor.  

The daily toiler at some noisy loom  
Draws back her garments from the kitchen aid;  
Meanwhile, the latter leans upon her broom,  
Unconscious of the bow the laundress made.  

The grocer’s daughter eyes the farmer’s lass  
With haughty glances, while the lawyer’s wife  
Would pay no visits to the trading class  
If policy were not her creed in life.  

The merchant’s son nods coldly at the clerk;  
The proud possessor of a pedigree  
Ignores the youth whose father rose through work;  
The title-seeking maiden scorns all three.  

The aristocracy of blood looks down  
Upon the “nouveau riche,” while, in disdain,  
The lovers of the intellectual frown  
On both and worship at the shrine of brain.  

“No classes here,” the clergyman has said;  
“We are one family.” Yet see his rage  
And horror when his favorite son would wed  
Some pure and pretty player on the stage.  

It is the vain yet natural way  
Of vaunting our weak selves, our pride, our worth!  
Not till the long-delayed millennial day  
Shall we behold “no classes” on God’s earth.
outputs.L2:
“Society has no ranks among us”?  
Such a claim is empty nonsense. The fashionable young man from the village mocks the rustic; beggars who plead through city streets regard those receiving parish aid as beneath them. A woman who spends her days tending a clattering loom draws her skirt away from the kitchen servant, while that servant, resting on her broom, fails to notice the deferential gesture offered by the washerwoman.

The shopkeeper’s daughter looks proudly upon the farmer’s girl. A lawyer’s wife would never socialize with merchants if practical advantage did not guide her conduct. The merchant’s son gives the clerk only a distant nod. A man proud of his ancestry refuses to acknowledge a young man whose father earned his position through labor, while a young woman eager to gain a title despises all three.

Those who claim nobility by birth look down on the newly wealthy. In turn, people who prize intellect regard both groups with contempt and bow only before mental achievement.

A minister declares, “There are no distinctions here; we are all one family.” Yet he reacts with fury and dismay when his cherished son wishes to marry a virtuous, beautiful actress.

This urge to proclaim our own importance, dignity, and superiority is foolish, though deeply human. Only when the long-awaited millennium finally arrives will the world truly be free of social classes.
outputs.L3:
The claim that society has “no classes” is revealed as little more than empty talk, since people constantly rank and judge one another according to their social position. Class consciousness is not confined to the rich or aristocratic; snobbery exists at every level of society. Workers, tradespeople, professionals, and the wealthy all tend to look down on those whom they consider socially inferior, even while resenting similar treatment from those above them.

These class distinctions depend on more than wealth or ancestry. A person may also be judged by occupation, public status, education, or intellectual achievement. As a result, society is divided by many overlapping forms of pride and prejudice. Even people who publicly advocate equality are not free from such attitudes. The clergyman, for example, may preach that all people are equal, yet his principles weaken when a personal or family relationship crosses an accepted class boundary. His reaction exposes the difference between professed beliefs and actual behavior.

The poem therefore presents class pride as a deeply rooted human weakness rather than a problem belonging to one particular social group. Almost everyone wants to feel superior to someone else, making genuine equality difficult to achieve. Its conclusion is pessimistic: class prejudice is unlikely to disappear in the present world and may survive until some distant, ideal future age in which human nature itself has changed.
outputs.L4:
The poem disputes the comforting claim that modern society has become classless. Instead, it presents a broad survey of social life, showing that nearly every group creates its own hierarchy and finds someone else to despise. People judge one another according to occupation, income, ancestry, education, manners, reputation, and intellectual standing. Those with wealth look down on the poor; those with distinguished families dismiss people of ordinary birth; professionals and tradespeople rank themselves against one another; and even writers, scholars, and other intellectuals divide into circles of supposed superiority. No matter where a person stands, there always seems to be another group beneath them against which they can measure their status.

Through this accumulation of examples, the poem suggests that class is not merely a formal division based on money or inherited rank. It is also a habit of mind: the desire to feel important by treating others as lesser. Even people who suffer from social prejudice may reproduce it by directing contempt toward someone still more vulnerable. Claims of equality therefore ring hollow, because distinctions of status continually reappear in new forms.

The poem ultimately identifies vanity and pride as the forces that sustain class prejudice. Human beings cling to any difference that allows them to imagine themselves superior, whether that difference involves wealth, birth, work, education, taste, or intelligence. For that reason, the poem offers little hope that class feeling will disappear through ordinary social progress. True equality belongs to an ideal future age—one in which people have finally overcome the pride that makes them divide the world into those above and those below.
outputs.L5:
### Why the Future Is Ours

Why do we keep moving forward, even when the path is uncertain? The answer lies in our ability to hope, learn, and grow. Every challenge gives us a chance to become stronger, while every success reminds us of what is possible.

The future is not something that simply happens to us. It is shaped by our choices, our actions, and our willingness to work together. When we understand why our efforts matter, we can create meaningful change—not only for ourselves, but for everyone around us.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical rhyming poem exposing the social hierarchies and class prejudices that persist despite claims that society has “no classes.”
counterfactuals.output:
### **A Classless Little Nation**

We live, they say, where class is dead—  
A quaint old ghost, long put to bed.  
No ranks remain, no gates, no tiers—  
Just better schools and auctioned peers.

The duke now wears a business suit,  
His crest replaced by “family loot.”  
He earned it all, as he’ll explain,  
Through Father’s firm and Grandpa’s gain.

The poor are free to rise, of course,  
Provided they can buy the horse;  
And all may dine where chandeliers  
Illuminate inherited careers.

No servants now! That word is crude—  
We have “support staff,” smartly shoed.  
They enter softly, clean the floor,  
Then vanish by the service door.

No accents mark the high from low—  
Though some mean “stop,” and some mean “go.”  
One voice is “warm”; one “lacks finesse”;  
One says “I’m rich” by saying less.

The wealthy practise being plain:  
They praise old boots and private planes.  
Their kitchens sport a rustic theme—  
Hand-carved by teams no guest has seen.

The middle ranks, with anxious grin,  
Keep judging who is out or in.  
They mock the rich, despise the poor,  
Then check the postcode next door.

The poor, we’re told, make foolish choices:  
Cheap food, bad loans, and louder voices.  
The rich choose wisely—tax relieved—  
And call each loophole “wealth achieved.”

At school, each child receives a chance:  
One gets a book; one gets finance,  
A tutor, flat, and uncle’s name—  
But merit wins the race the same.

At work, the ladder stands for all,  
Though some begin beside the wall;  
While some are placed upon the top  
And praised for knowing where to stop.

We have no classes—none at all!  
Just those who climb and those who fall;  
Those born to feast, those billed per crumb,  
And those who say, “We all can come.”

So raise a glass to equal ground,  
Where velvet ropes are all around;  
No upper class, no lower masses—  
Just “different kinds of social grasses.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a Victorian-style poem illustrating how nearly every social group looks down upon another, ending with the hope that class distinctions will disappear in the millennium.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Ladder of Contempt**

The lord looks down upon the squire,  
The squire upon the clerk;  
The clerk esteems the craftsman coarse,  
The craftsman scorns the work.  

The merchant mocks the scholar’s coat,  
The scholar jeers at trade;  
The soldier calls the parson meek,  
The parson mourns the blade.  

The city sneers at country speech,  
The village scoffs at town;  
The old condemn the young as rash,  
The young cry age is brown.  

The rich man names the poor man sloth,  
The poor man brands him stone;  
And each, to raise his little throne,  
Must thrust some neighbour down.  

The lady chides the serving-maid,  
The maid her mistress’ pride;  
The tenant rails against the lord,  
Yet rules his hearth beside.  

Thus, rank on rank, the nations climb  
A stair of dust and breath,  
While Time, the leveller, waits below,  
And smiles—and whispers, “Death.”  

But surely dawn shall gild the world  
When Love’s long reign is come,  
And none shall ask of blood or purse,  
Or palace, field, or slum;  

When “high” and “low” are words forgot,  
And Pride has lost dominion—  
All souls shall stand as equals then,  
In God’s bright millennium.
